title: Ἥρως
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 131 (= Perry 110). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἥρωά τις ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας ἔχων, τούτῳ πολυτελῶς ἔθυεν.
sentences.tr: Hērōa tis epi tēs oikias echōn, toutōi polytelōs ethyen.
sentences.l: A certain man, having a hero in his house, sacrificed to him lavishly.
sentences.n: A ἥρως is a dead man of power who is worshipped at the place that holds him; a household hero is the protecting spirit of that one house, and the man who has one has an obligation as well as a guardian. ἐπί with the genitive is the plain 'in, at' of place. θύω takes the dative of the god sacrificed to.

sentences.t: Ἀεὶ δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀναλισκομένου καὶ πολλὰ εἰς θυσίας δαπανῶντος, ὁ ἥρως ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ νύκτωρ ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, πέπαυσο τὴν οὐσίαν διαφθείρων· ἐὰν γὰρ πάντα ἀναλώσας πένης γένῃ, ἐμὲ αἰτιάσῃ. »
sentences.tr: Aei de autou analiskomenou kai polla eis thysias dapanōntos, ho hērōs epistas autōi nyktōr ephē· « All’, ō houtos, pepauso tēn ousian diaphtheirōn· ean gar panta analōsas penēs genēi, eme aitiasēi. »
sentences.l: But he being always at expense and laying out much upon sacrifices, the hero, having stood over him by night, said: « Come, you there, have done with destroying your substance; for if, having spent everything, you become poor, you will blame me. »
sentences.i: But since he was always at expense, laying out great sums on sacrifices, the hero stood over him one night and said: « Come now, you there — have done with ruining your estate. For if you spend it all and fall into poverty, you will lay the blame on me. »
sentences.n: ἐπιστάς, 'having stood over', is the regular verb for a god or a dream coming to a sleeper's side; it says nothing about standing up. ὦ οὗτος is a brusque way of hailing a man, 'you there'. πέπαυσο is a perfect middle imperative, 'be done with it', and 'stop doing' takes a supplementary participle, διαφθείρων, for the thing to be stopped. οὐσία is what a man has, his property. αἰτιάσῃ is future middle, second person singular: not a threat but a prediction.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ διὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀβουλίαν δυστυχοῦντες τὴν αἰτίαν ἐπὶ τοὺς θεοὺς ἀναφέρουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi dia tēn heautōn aboulian dystychountes tēn aitian epi tous theous anapherousin.
sentences.l: Thus many, faring badly through their own want of counsel, carry the blame up onto the gods.
sentences.n: ἀβουλία is the absence of βουλή, deliberation — not stupidity but the failure to think a thing through before doing it. ἀναφέρω ἐπί is to carry a charge up and set it on someone else, which is exactly what the hero foretold in the last line.
